segments.en: Two green peaks rise straight out of the sea, sharp as the tips of a crown. They're the Pitons, Gros Piton and Petit Piton, and when the sun sets behind them, the whole bay turns gold. Bonjou, and good evening from Saint Lucia.
Saint Lucia is a mountainous island in the eastern Caribbean, one of the Windward Islands. Its middle is covered in rainforest, and its edges are ringed with fishing villages and sandy coves.

That word bonjou you heard is Kwéyòl, the island's French-based Creole. English is the official language, but many Saint Lucians switch easily between the two, and Kwéyòl is heard at home, on the radio and in songs.

Why French? Because Britain and France fought over this island so many times that it changed hands again and again. People sometimes call it the Helen of the West Indies, after the beautiful Helen of Troy in the old Greek stories.

Near the town of Soufrière, you can visit a volcano you can drive into. Steam hisses from the ground, the air smells of sulphur, and further down the slope people wade into warm, muddy pools that are said to be good for the skin.
Deep in the forest lives the Saint Lucia parrot, found nowhere else on Earth, with a blue face, green wings and a flash of red on its chest. It's the national bird.
On Friday nights, head to Gros Islet for the street party known as the Jump Up. Music thumps from speakers, fish is grilled at the roadside, and neighbours and visitors dance together in the street.

The national dish is green fig and saltfish. Here, green fig means unripe bananas, boiled and served with salted cod, onions and peppers. Try some bakes, fried dough, or a hot bowl of bouyon, a thick soup full of vegetables.
Saint Lucia is small, but it has produced two Nobel prize winners, the economist Arthur Lewis and the poet Derek Walcott, whose poems are full of the sea and light of this island.
Music is everywhere, from calypso and soca at Carnival in July to the island's own sound, Dennery Segment, fast and full of energy.
Manners matter. Greet people before you ask them anything, and expect a warm answer. Sunday is a quiet family day, often with a big lunch after church.
Mèsi, thank you, for visiting. Sail south past the Pitons, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines is waiting with its string of little islands.
